units.title: Fluid Mechanics
units.intro: A **fluid** is anything that can flow: liquids and gases. Solids keep shape and volume; liquids keep volume but take the container’s shape; gases take both shape and volume and squash easily.

f1.title: Same water: ice below 0 °C, liquid, steam above 100 °C. Plasma is a fourth, ionised state.

f3.title: Gauge pressure is just ρgh. Absolute pressure adds the air sitting on the surface.

f4.title: Hydraulic press / jack / car brake: small force on small piston → large force on large piston.

f5.title: Apparent weight in a liquid = true weight − upthrust. That is the “loss of weight” in the textbook activity.

cards.title: Same water: ice below 0 °C, liquid, steam above 100 °C. Plasma is a fourth, ionised state.
1.1.1 States of Matter
body: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.
Solid iron, liquid water and helium gas are examples of different states of matter at room temperature.
A brick, for example, maintains its familiar shape and size day in and day out.
Solid materials expand with increasing temperatures, but they retain their shape.

cards.title: 1.1.2 Density and relative density
body: ρ = m / V unit kg/m³ (or g/cm³). Water: 1000 kg/m³ = 1 g/cm³.
**Relative density** (specific gravity) = density of substance ÷ density of water. No unit. A RD of 0.8 means “0.8 times as dense as water” — it will float.

cards.title: Mnemonic
body: Density is how *crowded* the mass is. Relative density is a comparison with water — drop the units and compare with 1.

cards.title: Exercise A — density
cards.problem: A stone has mass 75 g and volume 25 cm³. Find (i) density in g/cm³ (ii) relative density (iii) whether it sinks in water.

steps.text: **Required:** ρ, RD, sink or float. ρ = m/V = 75 / 25 = **3 g/cm³**.
RD > 1, so the stone is denser than water → **sinks**.
Same density in SI: 3 g/cm³ = 3000 kg/m³.

cards.answer: Same density in SI: 3 g/cm³ = 3000 kg/m³.

cards.title: 1.1.2 Density and Relative Density
body: Aeoroplanes are made chiefly of aluminium alloys.

The reasons for this difference lie at the atomic and nuclear levels.

cards.q: Which of the following states of matter possesses neither a definite volume nor a definite shape?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand physical properties of states of matter**
Solids have both definite shape and volume. Liquids have definite volume but indefinite shape. Gases have neither definite volume nor definite shape as their intermolecular bonds are extremely weak, permitting free molecular expansion.

**Step 2: Compare with options**
Therefore, the correct physical state matching the description is *

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which instrument is specifically designed to measure atmospheric pressure?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Operational review of pressure instruments**
A thermometer measures temperature. A manometer measures gauge pressure of a confined gas. A sphygmomanometer measures blood pressure. A barometer is specifically engineered to measure the ambient atmospheric pressure.

**Step 2: Conclusion**
Thus, the correct instrument is the **Barometer**.

cards.title: 1.2 Pressure
body: P = F / A Force must be perpendicular to the area. Unit: N/m² = **pascal (Pa)**. Also used: 1 atm = 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 76 cmHg.

Liquid pressure
body: At depth h in a liquid of density ρ:
P = ρ g h
Depends only on depth and density — not on the shape of the container. Same depth → same pressure (that is why dam walls are thicker at the bottom).
Absolute pressure under the atmosphere:
P = Pₐₜₘ + ρ g h

cards.title: Gauge pressure is just ρgh. Absolute pressure adds the air sitting on the surface.
Mnemonic — deeper, denser, heavier air
body: Pressure grows with *ρ*, *g* and *h*. Double the depth, double the liquid pressure. Salt water (bigger ρ) presses harder than fresh water at the same depth.

cards.title: Atmospheric pressure & applications
body: Air has weight, so it presses. A mercury barometer supports about 76 cm of Hg. Manometers (U-tubes) compare an unknown pressure with the atmosphere using a liquid column ρgh.
Everyday uses in the book: drinking with a straw (you lower pressure in your mouth; atmosphere pushes the drink up), syringes, siphons, pumps, dam design, hydraulic machines.

cards.title: 1.2.1 Pressure and its Units
body: A learner standing on his feet on the ground experiences pressure due to his weight on the ground.
The total force due to the weight of the learner remains the same but the pressure varies when the learner stands on one foot to when the learner stands on both feet.
The SI unit of pressure is newton per square metre (N/m2).
A block (a cuboid of mass with three different dimensions), a ruler and a spring balance.

Using a pin the learner poked several holes in the plastic while squeezing the bag gently.

cards.title: 1.2.3 Atmospheric Pressure
body: The force on 1000 square centimeters is about a ton!
Although air molecules are invisible, they still have weight and take up space.
Since there’s a lot of “empty” space between air molecules, air can be compressed to fit into a smaller volume.
When it’s compressed, air is said to be under high pressure.

cards.title: 1.2.4 Applications of Liquid and Atmospheric Pressure
body: The syringe and the rubber sucker function by means of atmospheric pressure.
A rubber sucker is a circular device with a concave surface.

When pressed flat against a smooth surface, such as glass, the natural spring of the rubber will try to regain the concave shape, but air pressure will force the surface to remain flattened against the glass for as long as there is no air leak to the underside.
Rubber suckers operate by atmospheric pressure.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The value of standard atmospheric pressure at sea level is equivalent to which of the following?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Standard constants**
Standard atmospheric pressure ($$P_{\\text{atm}}$$) at sea level is defined by international conventions to be exactly $$1\\, \\text{atm}$$.

**Step 2: Conversion to SI units**
$$1\\, \\text{atm} = 1.01325 \\times 10^5\\, \\text{N/m}^2 = 1.013 \\times 10^5\\, \\text{Pa}$$.
Therefore, the correct option is **$$1.013 \\times 10^5\\, \\text{Pa}$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which physical principle states that any change in pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to all portions of the fluid?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze statement definitions**
Archimedes' principle concerns buoyancy. Bernoulli's principle relates fluid speed to pressure in dynamic systems. Pascal's Principle explicitly defines the transmission of static pressure changes in enclosed, incompressible fluids.

**Step 2: Match principle**
Thus, the principle defined in the question is **Pascal's Principle**.

body: A change of pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls.

cards.title: Exercise C — hydraulic jack
cards.problem: A driver presses with 40 N on a piston of area 5 cm². The car sits on a piston of area 400 cm². What force lifts the car?

steps.text: **Given:** F₁ = 40 N, A₁ = 5 cm², A₂ = 400 cm².
Pascal: pressure is equal, so F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂.
Areas can stay in cm² — the ratio A₂/A₁ is the same in any unit as long as both match.
The jack multiplies the force 80 times.
The car’s weight that can be held is 3200 N (about 320 kg-force if g = 10).

cards.answer: The car’s weight that can be held is 3200 N (about 320 kg-force if g = 10).

cards.title: 1.3.1 Applications of Pascal’s Principle
body: Pascal’s principle became the basis for one of the most important machines ever developed, that is the hydraulic lift (press).
A simple hydraulic lift of the variety used to raise a car in an auto shop typically consists of two large cylinders side by side.
Valves control the flow of the fluid between the two cylinders.

When a person applies force by pressing down the piston in one cylinder (the input cylinder), this yields a uniform pressure that causes output in the second cylinder, pushing up a piston that raises the car.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The magnitude of the buoyant force acting on a submerged object is always equal to:

options.A: The weight of the submerged object
options.B: The volume of the submerged object
options.C: The weight of the fluid displaced by the object
options.D: The volume of the fluid displaced by the object

cards.why:
**Step 1: Apply Archimedes' Principle**
Archimedes' principle states that the buoyant force on a submerged body is equal in magnitude to the gravitational weight of the volume of fluid that the body displaces ($$F_B = m_f g = \\rho_f V_f g$$).

**Step 2: Select option**
Hence, the correct answer is **The weight of the fluid displaced by the object**.

cards.title: Quick check

options.A: Greater than the density of the liquid
options.B: Equal to or less than the density of the liquid
options.C: Exactly twice the density of the liquid

cards.why:
**Step 1: Formulate flotation requirements**
For flotation, the static vertical forces must be balanced ($$F_B = W$$). This mathematically requires:
$$\\frac{V_f}{V_o} = \\frac{\\rho_o}{\\rho_f} \\le 1.0$$

**Step 2: Deduce density constraints**
This ratio is only valid and stable at or near the surface if the object's average density ($$\\rho_o$$) is **equal to or less than the density of the liquid ($$\\rho_f$$)**.

cards.title: 1.4–1.5 Buoyancy, Archimedes, flotation
body: **Upthrust** (buoyant force) is the upward force a fluid exerts on a body. It exists because pressure on the bottom face is larger than on the top face (greater depth).
**Archimedes’ principle:** upthrust = weight of fluid displaced.
F_B = ρ_fluid × V_displaced × g

1.4–1.5 Buoyancy, Archimedes, flotation

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the relative density of pure water at $$4^\\circ\\text{C}$$?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze relative density formula**
$$\\text{Relative Density} = \\frac{\\rho_{\\text{substance}}}{\\rho_{\\text{water}}}$$

**Step 2: Substitute for pure water**
For pure water at $$4^\\circ\\text{C}$$, the substance is water itself:
$$\\text{Relative Density} = \\frac{\\rho_{\\text{water}}}{\\rho_{\\text{water}}} = 1.0$$
Thus, the relative density of pure water is **$$1.0$$**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: As depth in a static fluid increases, the hydrostatic pressure within the fluid:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Write hydrostatic pressure formula**
$$P = \\rho g h$$

**Step 2: Determine proportionality**
Since fluid density ($$\\rho$$) and gravitational acceleration ($$g$$) are constant, pressure $$P$$ is directly proportional to depth $$h$$. Thus, pressure **increases linearly** with depth.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Why do our ears pop when we climb high mountains?

options.A: The temperature decreases rapidly, compressing the eardrum
options.B: The external atmospheric pressure decreases below the internal ear pressure
options.C: The internal fluid density of the ear decreases
options.D: The gravitational force pulling on the ear increases

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze physical processes at altitude**
As altitude increases, atmospheric density and pressure drop exponentially.

**Step 2: Relate to inner ear pressure**
The air trapped inside the middle ear remains initially at the higher sea-level pressure. The imbalance (internal pressure > external atmospheric pressure) forces the eardrum outward until air escapes through the Eustachian tube, creating a "popping" sensation to restore equilibrium. Thus, the correct option is **The external atmospheric pressure decreases below the internal ear pressure**.

Thus, the correct option is **The external atmospheric pressure decreases below the internal ear pressure**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: A fully submerged stone sinks deeper into a deep pool of fresh water. What happens to the buoyant force acting on it?

options.D: It drops to zero at extreme depths

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze the variables in buoyant force formula**
$$F_B = \\rho_f V_o g$$

**Step 2: Evaluate constants**
Water density ($$\\rho_f$$) is essentially constant because liquids are highly incompressible. The volume of the submerged stone ($$V_o$$) and gravity ($$g$$) are constant. Therefore, the buoyant force **remains virtually constant** regardless of depth.

The upward force a fluid exerts on a body.
Density is a physical property of matter, as each element and compound has a unique density associated with it.

Solid is the state in which matter maintains a fixed volume and shape; liquid is the state in which matter maintains a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container; and gas is the state in which matter expands to occupy whatever volume is available.

tips.text: There are three accepted states of matter: solid, liquid and gas.

Solid is the state in which matter maintains a fixed volume and shape; liquid is the state in which matter maintains a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container; and gas is the state in which matter expands to occupy whatever volume is available.
Solids are not easily compressible and do not flow easily.
Liquids are not easily compressible but flow easily.
As the energy of the moving molecules overcomes the molecular forces of attraction, the material will change its state from solid to liquid to gas.
Solid iron, liquid water and helium gas are examples of different states of matter at room temperature.
The density of a substance is the total mass of the substance divided by its volume.
A concept related to density is the relative density (or specific gravity) of a material, which is the ratio of the material’s density to the density of water.
Relative density is a dimensionless quantity.
The density of any substance in grams per cubic centimetre is identical with the relative density; its density in kilograms per cubic metre is 1000 times its relative density.

similar.a: C. the water exerts an outward normal force on the object. — A fluid at rest exerts its pressure force perpendicular (normal) to every surface it touches (G12 p.11–15). C is the only option describing this, although the force of the water on the object is directed inward (onto the object's surface); 'outward' must be read as 'from the water, normal to the surface'. Answer: C.

cards.title: 2.1 The Structure of the Atom
body: An understanding of the structure of the atom and its interaction with energy helps in discoveries about matter.
Much of the study of modern physics is an attempt to understand the inner structure of the atom.
An atom is the smallest particle of an element which can take part in a chemical reaction.
The nucleus is the central core of an atom.
The nucleus is surrounded by electrons moving in orbits at various energy levels.

cards.title: 2.1 Atom — a picture good enough for this course
body: Nucleus (protons +, neutrons 0) with electrons in energy levels around it. Electrons do not sit anywhere — they occupy allowed orbits / shells. Jumping between levels absorbs or emits a packet of light.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following scientific figures is historically associated with the discovery of the electron in 1897?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Historical review of atomic structure**
John Dalton formulated early atomic theory. Ernest Rutherford discovered the atomic nucleus. Niels Bohr introduced quantized orbits. J.J. Thomson discovered the electron using cathode ray tube experiments in 1897.

**Step 2: Conclusion**
Therefore, J.J. Thomson is the correct scientist.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In 1932, James Chadwick discovered which of the following subatomic particles?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Track subatomic discoveries**
The electron was discovered in 1897 by Thomson. The proton was identified by Rutherford in 1918. James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932 by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles.

**Step 2: Conclusion**
Thus, James Chadwick discovered the neutron.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which atomic model envisioned the atom as a uniform positive sphere with embedded negative electrons?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Identify model definitions**
The planetary model has orbiting electrons. The Bohr model introduces energy quantization. The Plum Pudding model, proposed by J.J. Thomson, describes electrons embedded in a uniform positive sphere.

**Step 2: Match**
Thus, the correct model is the Plum pudding model.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze particle properties**
Electrons carry negative charge. Protons carry positive charge. Neutrons are electrically neutral.

**Step 2: Select charge**
Therefore, the charge of a neutron is exactly **Zero**.

cards.title: 2.2 Particle–wave duality & the photon
body: Light behaves as a wave (interference, diffraction) *and* as particles called **photons**.
E = h f also E = h c / λ
h = Planck’s constant = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. Higher frequency (bluer / UV) photons carry more energy. Radio photons are cheap and harmless one-by-one; X-ray photons are expensive.

cards.title: Mnemonic
body: Energy rides on frequency, not on “how bright”. Brightness = more photons, not fatter photons.

cards.title: 2.2.1 The Dual Nature of Light
body: A stone dropped into a lake (collision) and the ripples (wave motion) that spread out from its point of impact apparently have in common only the ability to carry energy and momentum from one place to another.
The concept that light travels as a series of little packets is directly opposed to the wave theory of light.
The wave theory of light explains diffraction and interference, which the quantum theory cannot account for.
The quantum theory explains the photoelectric effect, which the wave theory cannot account for.

cards.title: 2.2.2 Energy of a Photon
body: In the year 1865 James Clerk Maxwell (1831–1879), Scottish physicist, proposed that light is a high frequency electromagnetic wave.
According to his theory the speed of these electromagnetic waves is 3×108 m/s, which is in agreement with the measured value.
In his theory, he concluded that light is composed of corpuscles or discontinuous quanta of energy.
By increasing the intensity of the light of given wavelength, there is only an increase in the number of photons per second crossing a given area, with each photon having the same energy.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Photoelectric effect
body: When light hits some metals, electrons fly out — but only if the light’s frequency is above a **threshold frequency** f₀. Below that, even a very bright lamp does nothing. That wrecks the old wave-only model and is why Einstein used photons.
Kₘₐₓ = h f − φ
φ (work function) = minimum energy to free an electron = h f₀.

cards.title: One photon vs one electron. Extra energy becomes kinetic energy.
Raises Kₘₐₓ
body: Higher f (or shorter λ). Intensity does *not* change Kₘₐₓ.

cards.title: Raises number of electrons
body: Higher intensity (more photons per second) — but only if f ≥ f₀.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Photoelectric effect
body: Applications in the book: photocells, automatic doors / counters, solar exposure meters, sound-on-film, burglar alarms — anything that turns light into a current of electrons.

cards.title: Exercise E — photon energy
cards.problem: Violet light has frequency 7.5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Find the energy of one photon. h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

steps.text: (Do not use ½mv² here — that is the electron later.) E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴) × (7.5 × 10¹⁴). 6.63 × 7.5 = 49.725. 10⁻³⁴ × 10¹⁴ = 10⁻²⁰.
In electron-volts (optional extra): divide by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 3.1 eV.

cards.answer: In electron-volts (optional extra): divide by 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ ≈ 3.1 eV.

cards.title: Exercise F — photoelectric
cards.problem: A metal has work function 3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Light of frequency 8.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz shines on it. Find (i) whether electrons are emitted (ii) Kₘₐₓ.

steps.text: Threshold check equivalent: f₀ = φ/h = 3.2e-19 / 6.63e-34 ≈ 4.83×10¹⁴ Hz.
If the question had used a frequency below 4.83×10¹⁴ Hz, Kₘₐₓ would be “no emission”, not a negative number.

cards.answer: If the question had used a frequency below 4.83×10¹⁴ Hz, Kₘₐₓ would be “no emission”, not a negative number.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Photoelectric Effect
body: The phenomenon of photoelectric emission was discovered in 1887 by Heinrich Hertz, during his electromagnetic wave experiments.

In his experimental investigation, on the production of electromagnetic waves by means of a spark discharge, he observed that high voltage sparks across the detector loop were enhanced when the emitter (metal) plate was illuminated by ultraviolet light.

Lenard observed that when ultraviolet radiations were allowed to fall on the emitter plate, C (cathode) of an evacuated glass tube enclosing two electrodes (metal plates), current flows in the circuit (Fig. 2.5).
As soon as the ultraviolet radiations were stopped, the current flow was also stopped.

cards.title: 2.2.4 Applications of Photoelectric Effect
body: Photocell is a device used to convert light energy into electric energy.
Photocell is an application of the photoelectric effect.
When the light of a suitable wavelength falls on emitter C, photoelectrons emit instantaneously from the emitter.
Owing to the ionization of the inert gas, the current strength is more and it is five to ten times stronger than the current from the vacuum type.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The strong nuclear force within an atomic nucleus acts between which of the following?

options.D: Between any two nucleons (protons or neutrons) at close range

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze strong nuclear force properties**
The strong nuclear force is charge-independent. It does not affect electrons, which are leptons.

**Step 2: Assess options**
It acts equally between proton-proton, neutron-neutron, and proton-neutron pairs at extremely short distances ($$< 10^{-15}\\, \\text{m}$$). Therefore, it acts between any two nucleons.

cards.problem: The strong nuclear force within an atomic nucleus acts between which of the following?

steps.text: The strong nuclear force is charge-independent. It does not affect electrons, which are leptons.
It acts equally between proton-proton, neutron-neutron, and proton-neutron pairs at extremely short distances ($$< 10^{-15}\\, \\text{m}$$). Therefore, it acts between any two nucleons.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: According to the principle of wave-particle duality, light behaves as:

options.A: Exclusively a wave under all conditions
options.B: Exclusively a particle under all conditions
options.C: Both a wave and a particle depending on the experimental measurement
options.D: Neither a wave nor a particle

cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand wave-particle duality**
Light displays wave properties (like interference) during propagation and particle properties (like photoelectric effect) during energy exchange with matter.

**Step 2: Identify matching statement**
Thus, it behaves as both wave and particle depending on the experiment.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: According to the principle of wave-particle duality, light behaves as:

steps.text: Light displays wave properties (like interference) during propagation and particle properties (like photoelectric effect) during energy exchange with matter.
Thus, it behaves as both wave and particle depending on the experiment.

cards.title: 2.3 Atomic Spectra
body: Newton found that the spectrum of sunlight is impure because the different-coloured images overlap.
A pure spectrum is one in which the different-coloured images contain only the light of one colour.
The spectrometer (spectroscope) can be used to provide a pure spectrum.
A spectroscope may consist of a narrow slit, a prism, and several lenses that straighten the light rays and magnify the spectrum.
A spectroscope measures wavelengths accurately using either a diffraction grating or a prism to separate different wavelengths of light.

cards.title: 2.3 Atomic spectra
body: A hot gas or a discharge tube gives **line emission spectra** — only certain colours. A cool gas in front of white light gives dark **absorption lines** at those same frequencies. Each element has a fingerprint because its allowed electron jumps are unique.

cards.title: Jump story
body: Electron falls down a level → emits a photon of exactly that energy gap. Electron climbs up → absorbs that photon. No in-between colours.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What fundamental physical constant relates the energy of a photon to the frequency of its electromagnetic wave?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Recall the energy formula**
$$E = hf$$

**Step 2: Identify constant $$h$$**
$$h$$ is defined as Planck's constant ($$6.63 \\times 10^{-34}\\, \\text{J}\\cdot\\text{s}$$). This constant relates a photon's energy to its wave frequency.

steps.text: $$h$$ is defined as Planck's constant ($$6.63 \\times 10^{-34}\\, \\text{J}\\cdot\\text{s}$$). This constant relates a photon's energy to its wave frequency.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: In the photoelectric effect, if the frequency of the incident light is below the threshold frequency:

options.A: Electrons are emitted with very low kinetic energy
options.B: No electrons are emitted, regardless of the light intensity
options.C: Electrons are emitted after a long time lag

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze quantum threshold rules**
If $$f < f_0$$, the energy of each incident photon ($$hf$$) is strictly less than the metal's work function ($$\\phi_0$$).

**Step 2: Deduce outcomes**
Because the interaction is strictly one-on-one (one photon to one electron), no individual electron can gather enough energy to escape, regardless of how many photons hit the surface per second (intensity). Thus, **no electrons are emitted**.

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: In the photoelectric effect, if the frequency of the incident light is below the threshold frequency:

steps.text: If $$f < f_0$$, the energy of each incident photon ($$hf$$) is strictly less than the metal's work function ($$\\phi_0$$).

Because the interaction is strictly one-on-one (one photon to one electron), no individual electron can gather enough energy to escape, regardless of how many photons hit the surface per second (intensity). Thus, **no electrons are emitted**.

Spectroscopy is the technique of analysing light and correlating the analysis with the nature of the light source.

tips.text: An atom is composed of electrons, protons, and neutrons.
The protons and neutrons are the constituent particles of the nucleus, which is the central core of an atom.
The notations, respectively, Z, A, and N are used to represent the atomic number, mass number and neutron number, respectively.
The force that keeps the neutrons and protons within the nucleus is called the nuclear force. This force is greater than the force of repulsion between protons–protons at short range.
Atoms differ in kind by their atomic number.
Electromagnetic radiation and electrons have a dual nature. They behave as particles and as wave motion.
Einstein proposed in his theory that light is composed of corpuscles or discontinuous quanta of energy called “photons”.
Photons are electrically neutral and are not deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
The phenomenon of the emission of electrons from a metal surface when a radiation of suitable frequency incidents on it is known as the “photoelectric effect”.
The minimum frequency of the radiation required for electron emission is called the threshold frequency.
Raises Kₘₐₓ: Higher f (or shorter λ). Intensity does not change Kₘₐₓ.
Raises number of electrons: Higher intensity (more photons per second) — but only if f ≥ f₀.
